name: Designing Experiments and Using Simulations
title: Designing Experiments and Using Simulations
answer: Designing experiments and using simulations is a teaching approach where a school configured AI tool coaches students through the hardest parts of scientific thinking, asking what they will change, what they will keep the same, and how they will know if their idea was right. Simulations let students explore what would be dangerous, expensive, or impossible in a real lab, with the AI prompting predictions before each run and observations after. Misconception probes give teachers a picture of what students really believe before a lesson, so planning starts from actual understanding rather than assumption.

sections.body: Designing a good experiment is one of the hardest skills in science, and students often test too many things at once, forget a control, or pick a measure that cannot answer their question. A school configured tool can act as a coach in that moment, asking the questions a good teacher would ask, such as what the student will change, what they will keep the same, and how they will know if their idea was right. The student still designs the experiment, and the coach supplies the prompting rather than the answer. Simulations extend the same coaching into territory a real lab cannot reach, because they let students explore what would be dangerous, expensive, or impossible. The prediction step is what makes this work, since it turns clicking into thinking.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a classroom, the AI coach sits alongside the student's own experimental design, asking about the variable to change, the conditions to hold constant, and the evidence that would confirm or refute the idea. With simulations, students predict what will happen before each run and describe what they notice afterward, so a virtual planet with different gravity or a chemical reaction repeated many times becomes a thinking exercise rather than a game. For teachers, misconception probes work as a planning tool: the teacher asks an AI tool for short questions aimed at common misunderstandings, such as believing that heavier objects fall faster, and students answer before the lesson. The teacher then uses those results to plan instruction. The text does not give separate grade band guidance, so the same pattern of coach questions, prediction before simulation runs, and pre lesson probes applies across the science, STEM, and computer science settings described.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text gives no study, figure, or formal evidence label for this idea. It rests on practice rather than research as stated, describing what a school configured tool can do and how teachers can use misconception probes. The claims are about classroom use, not measured outcomes.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The teacher checks each misconception probe question for accuracy, because a poorly worded probe can plant the very misconception it was meant to find. The student designs the experiment, and the coach only asks questions, so the intellectual work stays with the learner. The prediction step must be preserved in simulations, otherwise the activity becomes clicking rather than thinking. These decisions about question quality, experiment ownership, and prediction remain with the teacher and student, not the tool.
